extracted.intended_audience: Title IX coordinators, educational institution administrators, compliance officers, and legal counsel (K-12 and postsecondary)
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance on the required procedures, protections, and limitations for recipients' responses to reports of Title IX sexual harassment, including supportive measures, investigatory and adjudicatory safeguards, evidence rules, hearings, notice, timeliness, and appeals. Applicable to both K-12 and postsecondary institutions with some provisions specific to postsecondary hearings and advisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of non-responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A presumption that the respondent is not responsible prior to a determination through the grievance process (§106.45(b)(1)(iv)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption is not a presumption of credibility or truthfulness for respondents; §106.45(b)(1)(ii) prohibits drawing any inferences about credibility based on status as complainant or respondent. The Department believes the presumption does not deprive complainants of protections already required under §106.44(a) and §106.45.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon notice of sexual harassment, recipients must promptly offer supportive measures to complainants (and may offer to respondents) with or without a formal complaint (§106.44(a); §106.30 defining 'supportive measures').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures are individualized services designed to protect safety and preserve equal access to education; they must not be punitive or disciplinary. Recipients must engage in an interactive discussion with the complainant to arrive at helpful supportive measures. Supportive measures should be kept confidential to the extent that confidentiality does not impair the ability to provide them (§106.30). A warning to a respondent about retaliation may be part of supportive measures because it is not punitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and burden on recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: The recipient—not the complainant—bears the burden to gather evidence and to prove whether the respondent committed sexual harassment (§106.45(b)(1)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection of a standard of proof is important and signals the degree of certainty required; articulating a specific standard helps ensure meaningful procedural safeguards. The Department reiterates the burden is on the recipient in the final regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disciplinary action before grievance process except exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may not take disciplinary or punitive action against a respondent without following a grievance process that complies with §106.45; exceptions exist for emergency removals and for sanctions imposed through an authorized informal resolution (§106.44; §106.45(b)(1); §106.45(b)(9); §106.44(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures that burden a respondent may be imposed so long as the burden is not unreasonable. Emergency removal under §106.44(c) permits removal from education programs in emergency situations without a completed grievance process; administrative leave for employee-respondents may also apply (§106.44(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence relevance and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance determinations must be based on relevant evidence only; certain types of evidence are deemed irrelevant or excluded (e.g., a complainant's prior sexual history, medical/psychological records, privileged information, and, for postsecondary adjudications, party or witness statements not subjected to cross-examination at a live hearing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes objective evaluation of relevant evidence and provides specific categories of excluded evidence to protect parties' privacy and ensure fair consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live hearing and cross-examination (postsecondary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Postsecondary institution recipients must provide a live hearing at which each party has an opportunity to cross-examine the other party; cross-examination must be conducted by party advisors (§106.45(b)(6)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a live hearing is required, cross-examination is considered critical to assessing credibility; if a party does not have an advisor, the recipient must provide one for the purpose of conducting cross-examination. Cross-examination conducted by advisors may require temporary delay of the hearing, which may constitute good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written questions when no live hearing (elementary and secondary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no hearing is held in elementary and secondary schools, parties have the opportunity to submit written questions to the other party, including questions designed to test credibility (§106.45(b)(6)(ii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision ensures parties can challenge credibility in settings where live hearings are not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to advisor of choice and equal treatment of lawyers
rubrics_metrics.description: Both parties have the right to select an advisor of choice and, if a school allows lawyers to participate, it must do so equally for both parties (§106.45(b)(2); 2011 Dear Colleague Letter discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial notice of allegations must advise parties of the right to an advisor and of the range of supportive measures available. Any restrictions on advisors' participation must apply equally to both parties. Recipients should consider disparity in ability to retain counsel; while not required to provide attorneys, recipients may choose to provide legal representation or advisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and reasonably prompt timeframes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must designate reasonably prompt timeframes for the grievance process (§106.45(b)(1)(v)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When delaying or extending timeframes for good cause, recipients must send written notice to both parties describing the delay or extension and the reasons (§106.45(b)(1)(v)). The Department's experience shows a typical adequate investigation often takes approximately 60 calendar days, and that investigations typically take longer than 20 days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice requirements and subsequent notice when allegations change
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must provide written notice to parties of allegations, of interviews/meetings relating to the allegations, and must provide subsequent written notices when the allegations under investigation change (§106.45(b)(2); §106.45(b)(5)(v); Mathews balancing discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial notice must inform parties of the right to an advisor and the recipient's grievance process and supportive measures; written notice of interviews/meetings is required. Providing subsequent notice reduces the risk of erroneous outcomes and satisfies due process considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of evidence and investigative report
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must provide parties and their advisors a copy of the evidence subject to inspection and review and must send the investigative report to each party and their advisors (§106.45(b)(5)(vi); §106.45(b)(5)(vii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department revised §106.45(b)(5)(vii) to require delivery of the investigative report for the same reasons evidence inspection is required: to ensure fairness and allow parties to meaningfully respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rape-shield protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures provide protections limiting questions and evidence inquiring into a complainant's prior sexual behavior (rape-shield protections) (§106.45(b)(6)(i)-(ii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These protections apply for complainants' benefit and restrict use of prior sexual history except in narrowly defined, relevant circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal appeal rights for dismissal decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Both parties are expressly granted equal rights to appeal a recipient's mandatory or discretionary dismissal decisions (§106.45(b)(8)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change recognizes that respondents may seek appellate review of dismissals where allegations might implicate Title IX jurisdiction and procedural protections; parties must be treated equally in appeal rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may adopt additional rules applied equally
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may adopt rules that apply to their grievance process beyond those required under §106.45, so long as such additional rules apply equally to both parties (introductory sentence of §106.45(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include reasonable rules of order and decorum for live hearings. Any additional rules must not undermine required protections and must be applied equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of supportive measures and Title IX Coordinator notice requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must keep the provision of supportive measures confidential to the extent that confidentiality does not impair ability to provide the measures; recipients must prominently display Title IX Coordinator contact information on their websites (§106.30; §106.8(b)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless a supportive measure affects the respondent in a way that requires disclosure of the complainant's identity (e.g., mutual no-contact order), the coordinator need not disclose the complainant's identity when selecting and implementing measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on drawing credibility inferences from status
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are expressly prohibited from drawing any inference about the credibility of a party based on that party's status as a complainant or respondent (§106.45(b)(1)(ii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prohibition is distinct from the presumption of non-responsibility and helps ensure fact-finders evaluate credibility based on evidence, not status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator signing formal complaint: discretionary initiation
rubrics_metrics.description: A Title IX Coordinator may sign a formal complaint initiating a grievance process even if the complainant does not wish to proceed, but only when the Coordinator determines signing is not clearly unreasonable under the known circumstances (Formal Complaint subsection of §106.30 definitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision to initiate proceedings against the complainant's wishes must be undertaken carefully, balancing complainant interests and institutional obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation of investigations for employees who leave and ESEA/ESSA considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations may continue even if the accused employee has left employment; ESEA/ESSA may require certain steps with respect to employees accused of sexual misconduct, and continuing investigations can help determine whether probable cause exists for misconduct findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients subject to ESEA should consider statutory obligations when deciding to continue investigations after an employee departs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retaliation protections and limits on abusive speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Retaliation prohibitions protect complainants and respondents; abuse of speech unprotected by the First Amendment that amounts to intimidation, threats, or coercion to chill Title IX rights is prohibited retaliation (§106.71 discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must take steps to prevent retaliation and take strong responsive actions if retaliation occurs; protections for free speech at public institutions are acknowledged but do not shield unlawful retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process balancing and requirement to provide meaningful notice and hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures must account for constitutional due process by balancing private interests, administrative burden, and likelihood additional procedures reduce erroneous outcomes; at minimum, parties facing severe sanctions require notice and an opportunity to be heard appropriate to the case (Mathews v. Eldridge; Goss v. Lopez references).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains written notice when allegations change and other procedural safeguards are necessary to reduce erroneous outcomes and satisfy fairness; courts emphasize notice and meaningful hearing appropriate to the nature of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on use of pre-investigation questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions posed to a respondent about an alleged incident prior to a formal complaint may not be used as part of an investigation or adjudication if a formal complaint is later filed, because parties must be given written notice of interviews and a recipient is precluded from imposing sanctions without following §106.45 grievance process (§106.45(b)(5)(v)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protects respondents from being improperly prejudiced by pre-formal-complaint interviews that were not conducted as part of the formal grievance process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisors provided by recipient may create good-cause delays
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient's temporary delay of a hearing caused by the need to provide an advisor to conduct cross-examination on behalf of a party may constitute good cause for extension of timeframes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should proactively determine whether a party will require an advisor provided by the recipient in advance of the hearing to avoid unnecessary delays; written notice of delay and reasons is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection with FERPA when handling student records
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must consider the intersection between these regulations and FERPA (34 CFR 99.3) when handling educational records and privacy issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble directs readers to the §106.6(e) FERPA subsection for further discussion of how FERPA obligations interact with Title IX requirements, particularly regarding confidentiality and disclosure of records.
